\textbf{Source.} Tadelis (2013), \emph{Game Theory: An Introduction}, Exercise 8.4 ``Industry Leader'', p.~170 {[}PDF 189{]}. Reproduced verbatim. (Gibbons Problem 2.6, p.~133, poses the same game and asks only for the subgame-perfect outcome.) Answer in the source: none in the book (the preface, p.~xiii, says about half are solved on Princeton UP's website; not checked).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Industry Leader:} Three oligopolists operate in a market with inverse demand given by \(P(Q) = a - Q\), where \(Q = q_1 + q_2 + q_3\), and \(q_i\) is the quantity produced by firm \(i\). Each firm has a constant marginal cost of production, \(c\), and no fixed cost. The firms choose their quantities dynamically as follows: Firm 1, which is the industry leader, chooses \(q_1 \geq 0\). Firms 2 and 3 observe \(q_1\) and then simultaneously choose \(q_2\) and \(q_3\), respectively.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  How many proper subgames does this dynamic game have? Explain briefly.
\item
  Is it a game of perfect or imperfect information? Explain briefly.
\item
  What is the subgame-perfect equilibrium of this game? Show that it is unique.
\item
  Find a Nash equilibrium that is not a subgame-perfect equilibrium.
\end{enumerate}
\end{quote}
